sa.prompt: List the six core variables required to design an interval training prescription, and explain why inserting recovery intervals enables greater total high-intensity workload compared to continuous training.
sa.model: The six core variables of an interval training prescription are: (1) Rate (intensity) of the exercise interval; (2) Distance or duration of the exercise interval; (3) Number of repetitions and sets; (4) Duration of the rest or active recovery interval; (5) Type of activity during recovery; and (6) Weekly training frequency. Inserting recovery intervals enables greater total high-intensity workload because rest periods allow partial resynthesis of intramuscular phosphagens (ATP and PCr), partial clearance and buffering of accumulated hydrogen ions and lactate, and restoration of acute neuromuscular drive. This prevents early exhaustion, allowing the athlete to accumulate significantly more time at peak intensity than possible during uninterrupted continuous exertion.
criteria: List all 6 core interval variables (intensity, distance/duration, reps/sets, rest duration, recovery activity type, frequency).

sa.prompt: Explain the physiological rules for monitoring recovery heart rates during interval training, including the standard range for athletes age 30 or younger, the age-adjustment formula for older athletes, and the inter-set recovery threshold.
sa.model: During interval training, recovery intervals are dictated by heart rate recovery rather than fixed clocks alone. For athletes age 30 or younger, the work interval re-entry threshold requires heart rate to drop to between 130 and 150 beats/min before starting the next repetition. For athletes over 30 years of age, age-related declines in maximal heart rate (~1 beat/min/year) require adjusting recovery boundaries by subtracting (Age - 30) from both limits. For example, a 45-year-old athlete subtracts 15 beats/min, yielding a target re-entry range of 115 to 135 beats/min. Additionally, between sets of repetitions, inter-set rest must be long enough for heart rate to drop below 120 beats/min.
criteria: State the standard re-entry range for age <= 30 (130 to 150 beats/min).
Provide the age-adjustment formula for age > 30 (subtract [Age - 30] from recovery limits) with a concrete example.

sa.prompt: Describe the origins, structure, and physiological benefits of Fartlek training and Scandinavian Interval-Circuit training.
sa.model: Fartlek training ('speed play') originated in Sweden in the 1930s as a continuous workout where the athlete unscriptedly alters running pace across varied natural terrain (hills, trails). Its continuous nature engages phosphagen, glycolytic, and oxidative energy systems concurrently, enhancing terrain adaptability and psychological engagement. Scandinavian Interval-Circuit training was developed in the 1960s/1970s, featuring a 3,000 to 10,000 m course with exercise stations every 400 to 1,600 m. Athletes jog/sprint between stations, stopping at each to perform strength, flexibility, or muscular endurance exercises before resuming running. It develops concurrent aerobic capacity, muscular endurance, and functional strength.
